questions.question: A server's Security log shows event 4624 for account t.vasile with Logon Type 10 and Source Network Address 198.51.100.24. How did this session reach the server?

options.text: Through a file share or another network resource opened from 198.51.100.24, with no desktop on the server
Through Remote Desktop from 198.51.100.24, giving the user an interactive desktop on the server
At the server's own keyboard, with 198.51.100.24 being the domain controller that checked the password
By unlocking a session that t.vasile had already opened on the server earlier

explanation.correct: Logon Type 10 (RemoteInteractive) is a logon through Terminal Services / Remote Desktop, and Source Network Address is the client the connection came from. The other common types: 2 Interactive (local console), 3 Network (for example an SMB share or other network access), 5 Service, 7 Unlock, 9 NewCredentials, 11 CachedInteractive. Next steps for an analyst: is t.vasile expected to RDP to this server, and from that address? The session's end is found by matching the Logon ID of this 4624 with 4647/4634.

distractors.a: Opening a share or another network resource is Logon Type 3 (Network): no desktop session is created.
distractors.c: A console logon is Logon Type 2. The Source Network Address field is the address the logon came from, not the domain controller that validated it.
distractors.d: Unlocking an existing session is Logon Type 7 (Unlock).

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can turn a logon type number into the access path, the basis of every lateral-movement question.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: 4624(S) An account was successfully logged on

questions.question: An analyst pivots on event 4688 to see how cmd.exe was launched on a workstation. Every 4688 event has New Process Name and Creator Process Name filled in, but the Process Command Line field is empty. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The processes ran with elevated rights, and Windows deliberately leaves out the arguments of elevated processes
Sysmon is not installed on the workstation, and event 4688 takes its command-line data from Sysmon
'Include command line in process creation events' is not enabled, so 4688 is written without arguments
The Security log rolled over, and Windows trims older events down to their mandatory fields

explanation.correct: Event 4688 needs the Audit Process Creation subcategory (Detailed Tracking). The command line is a separate setting, Administrative Templates\System\Audit Process Creation\Include command line in process creation events, which is not enabled by default; without it the Process Command Line field stays empty. Since 4688 events exist here, process-creation auditing is on and only the command-line setting is missing. Enabling it helps future events only: past arguments cannot be recovered from the Security log, so look at other sources such as Sysmon Event ID 1 (CommandLine), EDR telemetry or PowerShell logs.

distractors.a: Elevation is recorded in the Token Elevation Type field; it does not suppress the command line.
distractors.b: 4688 is written by Windows auditing. Sysmon writes its own Event ID 1 to a separate log; the two do not depend on each other.
distractors.d: Rollover removes whole events, oldest first. It does not strip fields from the events that remain.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know which logging has to be switched on before an incident for a question to be answerable.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Command line process auditing
Microsoft Learn: 4688(S) A new process has been created

questions.question: For a bank's internal audit you must state how long employee r.dinu was connected through Remote Desktop to a payments jump server on a given day. That day's Security log holds three 4624 events with Logon Type 10 for r.dinu and several 4647 and 4634 events. How do you pair each logon with its logoff?

options.text: Pair each 4624 with the next 4634 or 4647 for r.dinu in time order, since a user can hold only one session at a time
Match the Source Port of each 4624 with the port in the logoff events, since each RDP connection uses its own port
Use the 4648 events, which record the start and the end of every session opened with explicit credentials
Match the Logon ID of each 4624 with the Logon ID in 4647/4634 on the same server, and check for reboots in between

explanation.correct: The Logon ID (New Logon\Logon ID, field TargetLogonId) identifies one logon session; 4647 (user initiated logoff) and 4634 (session terminated) carry the same value. Microsoft notes that Logon IDs are only unique between reboots on the same computer, so check for a restart inside the window before pairing. For Remote Desktop and console sessions you will usually see both 4647 and 4634 when the user logs off. Session length = logoff time minus logon time for the same Logon ID. A 4624 with no matching logoff means the session was still open, was disconnected rather than logged off, or the log ended: report that as such instead of guessing.

distractors.a: A user can hold several sessions at once (reconnections, network logons, other tools), so pairing by time order can mix sessions and produce a wrong duration.
distractors.b: Logoff events carry no source port; the port is not a session key.
distractors.c: 4648 is logged on the machine where explicit credentials were supplied, at the attempt; it has no session end.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you correlate on the session key rather than on user names and timestamps when the numbers go into an audit report.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: 4634(S) An account was logged off
Microsoft Learn: 4647(S) User initiated logoff

questions.question: A bank's GPO enables Success auditing for the 'Audit File System' subcategory on file server FS-TREAS01. While investigating who opened files in D:\Shares\Treasury\M&A, you find no 4663 events for that folder, although other events are logged normally. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: The folder has no SACL entries matching the accounts and access types of interest, so nothing was generated
Event 4663 is only written on domain controllers; member file servers record file access as event 5140 instead
Event 4663 is only generated for failed access, so successful reads are never audited by this subcategory
The files were opened over the network, and 4663 only records access by programs running locally on the server itself

explanation.correct: Audit File System generates events only for objects that have a SACL whose entries match the account and the type of access (read, write, delete...). The default file-system SACLs generate nothing, so switching the subcategory on is not enough. For future cases, define audit entries on the sensitive folder (for example Success for Read data and Write data). For the current case, look at other sources that may exist: share access 5140/5145 if file-share auditing was enabled, endpoint or EDR telemetry, DLP. In an interview, say clearly that without the SACL the Security log cannot tell you who opened those files.

distractors.b: 4663 is written on any Windows computer that holds the audited object. 5140 is a different event (a network share was accessed) from a different subcategory, Audit File Share.
distractors.c: 4663 records access rights that were actually used and has no failure events; a failed attempt appears as 4656.
distractors.d: Access over SMB is checked on the server against the same SACL and is audited like local access; the subject is the remote user's network logon session.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know that object-access auditing needs both the policy and a SACL before you promise anyone a list of who opened a file.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Audit File System
Microsoft Learn: 4663(S) An attempt was made to access an object

questions.question: After a near miss, a bank wants Windows Security log evidence of files written to USB sticks on branch PCs that have no endpoint DLP agent. The team has enabled 'Audit File System' and plans to add a SACL to each stick when it is plugged in. What is the better design?

options.text: Keep the plan, and add a startup script that sets a SACL on drive letters D: to Z: at every boot
Enable 'Audit PNP Activity' only, because event 6416 lists the files that were copied to the newly connected device
Enable 'Audit Removable Storage', which audits files on removable media with no per-object SACL, then test it
Enable 'Audit Detailed File Share', because Windows presents a USB stick to the system as a local share

explanation.correct: Microsoft describes Audit Removable Storage as auditing attempts to access file system objects on a removable storage device, with an event for all objects and all access types and no dependency on the object's SACL. Successful reads and writes are logged as 4663 and failures as 4656. The SACL plan breaks down because many sticks are formatted FAT32 or exFAT, which have no security descriptors to hold a SACL, and drive letters change. After rollout, test with a sample stick on each Windows build in use, filter on WriteData/AppendData to cut read noise, and pair it with Audit PNP Activity (6416) to know which device was connected.

distractors.a: FAT32/exFAT sticks carry no ACLs at all, and drive letters are reassigned, so many writes would never be audited.
distractors.b: 6416 records that a new external device was recognised (Device ID, Vendor IDs, class). It contains no file names.
distractors.d: Detailed File Share (5145) covers access to network shares on the server that hosts them; a local USB volume is not reached through a share.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you design logging around the evidence you will need, and know which subcategory produces it.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Audit Removable Storage
Microsoft Learn: Monitor the use of removable storage devices

questions.question: On a workstation you find the 4624 event below. What does it establish about the account adm-backup?
questions.context:
EventID=4624 Computer=WS-ENG-042
SubjectUserName=d.lungu
TargetUserName=d.lungu TargetDomainName=CORP
LogonType=9 LogonProcessName=seclogo AuthenticationPackageName=Negotiate
TargetOutboundUserName=adm-backup TargetOutboundDomainName=CORP

options.text: adm-backup logged on interactively at WS-ENG-042's console, and a domain controller verified its password at that same moment
d.lungu's account was renamed to adm-backup, which is why both names appear in the same event
adm-backup was added to d.lungu's token as a group, giving d.lungu all of its privileges on this workstation
d.lungu keeps the local identity; adm-backup was attached for outbound connections only and is not proven valid here

explanation.correct: Logon Type 9 (NewCredentials) means the caller cloned its token and specified new credentials for outbound connections: the session keeps the same local identity (TargetUserName d.lungu), and the alternate account appears in Network Account Name (TargetOutboundUserName). LogonProcessName seclogo points to the Secondary Logon service, the path used by 'runas /netonly'. Those credentials are only used when the process connects to another system, so this event does not prove they were valid. Look on the destinations instead: 4624 (usually type 3) for adm-backup on servers, and authentication events on domain controllers, around the same time. Pass-the-hash tools that start a process with injected credentials produce the same pattern, so treat it as suspicious if adm-backup is not an account d.lungu is supposed to use.

distractors.a: An interactive logon is type 2. A NewCredentials logon does not check the alternate credentials with a domain controller when the session is created.
distractors.b: A rename is a separate account-management event; here both names are present because one is the local identity and the other the outbound credential.
distractors.c: 4624 does not record group changes, and adm-backup's rights apply only to connections to other systems, not to the local token.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know that the account in a NewCredentials logon is only claimed locally and has to be confirmed where it was used.

MITRE ATT&CK T1550.002 Pass the Hash

questions.subtopic: process tree reconstruction and PID reuse
questions.question: You are rebuilding a process tree from 4688 events on a server that has run for 40 days without a reboot. A suspicious rundll32.exe started at 14:10 on 3 March has Creator Process ID 0x1A2C and Creator Process Name powershell.exe. Searching New Process ID 0x1A2C returns two powershell.exe 4688 events: one on 11 February (a monitoring script run by svc_mon) and one at 14:06 on 3 March (user k.ilie, command line with -EncodedCommand). Which conclusion is sound?

options.text: The 3 March 14:06 instance: a PID is reused once its process exits, so the latest holder before 14:10 is the parent
The 11 February instance, because a process ID stays bound to the first process that received it until the next reboot
Neither: Creator Process ID holds the session's Logon ID, so the parent must be found through the 4624 events instead
It cannot be decided from 4688, because Creator Process ID is written in hex while New Process ID is written in decimal

explanation.correct: Windows reuses process IDs once a process has exited, so on a long-running server one PID can belong to many processes over time. Two processes cannot hold the same PID at the same time: the 11 February instance must have ended before the PID was given to the 14:06 instance, which makes the latest holder before 14:10 the parent. Confirm it with a second key: the Logon ID of rundll32's creator subject should match k.ilie's session, the same one seen in the 14:06 powershell.exe event. Sysmon Event ID 1 avoids the problem altogether: its ProcessGuid (and ParentProcessGuid) is a unique value per process, documented by Microsoft as making correlation easier.

distractors.b: A PID is not reserved until reboot; it returns to the pool as soon as the process exits.
distractors.c: Creator Process ID is the process ID of the process that ran the new process. The Logon ID is a separate field.
distractors.d: Both fields are hexadecimal in 4688, so they can be compared directly; conversion to decimal is only needed to compare with tools such as Task Manager.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know PIDs are not unique over time and verify parent links with a second key.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: 4688(S) A new process has been created
Microsoft Learn: Sysmon (Sysinternals)

questions.question: During a fraud investigation, a bank branch employee states that they never use administrator rights on their PC. You find the 4688 event below on that PC. What does it show?
questions.context:
EventID=4688 Computer=BR-PC-221
Account Name: s.marin
New Process Name: C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
Token Elevation Type: %%1937
Mandatory Label: S-1-16-12288

options.text: cmd.exe ran with a limited token at medium integrity, which is consistent with the employee's statement
cmd.exe ran as SYSTEM, so malware or a service rather than the user must have started it on the PC
s.marin started cmd.exe elevated at high integrity, as 'Run as administrator' does, so the account held admin rights
A UAC prompt appeared and was declined by the user, and Windows logged the attempt just before it cancelled the process

explanation.correct: %%1937 is Token Elevation Type 2: an elevated token with no privileges removed, used when UAC is on and the user starts a program with 'Run as administrator' (or the program always requires admin and the user is in Administrators). Mandatory Label S-1-16-12288 is High integrity. The event therefore puts an elevated, administrative cmd.exe under s.marin, which contradicts the statement. Next steps: how the account obtained admin rights (local Administrators membership; 4732 if group changes were audited), what the elevated cmd.exe launched (child 4688 events whose Creator Process ID equals its New Process ID), and whether the session was really the employee's (Logon ID back to 4624, logon type and source). Report what the account did; who sat at the keyboard is a separate question.

distractors.a: A limited token is %%1938 (Type 3) and medium integrity is S-1-16-8192; neither appears here.
distractors.b: System integrity is S-1-16-16384 and the account would be SYSTEM; the event shows s.marin at High integrity.
distractors.d: 4688 is written when a process is created. A declined UAC prompt creates no elevated process, so there would be no such event.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you read token fields precisely, which matters when the evidence may reach HR or court.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: 4688(S) A new process has been created

questions.subtopic: 4104 script block logging and encoded commands
questions.question: At a software company, an alert shows a process event with the command line 'powershell.exe -NoProfile -EncodedCommand <long Base64 string>'. Script block logging is enabled by policy on the host. Where is the most reliable place to read the code PowerShell actually ran?

options.text: Decode the Base64 string from the command line; that string is the complete code that the PowerShell process executed
The PSReadLine console history file, which keeps every command run by any PowerShell process on the host
The PowerShell transcript, which Windows writes by default to each user's Documents folder for every session
Event 4104 in the PowerShell Operational log, which records each script block as compiled, including run-time code

explanation.correct: -EncodedCommand carries Base64 of UTF-16LE text, and decoding it shows only the outer layer. Obfuscated scripts often build further code while running (decompression, string building, Invoke-Expression), and that code is not in the command line. With script block logging, PowerShell records the content of every script block it processes as event 4104, and Microsoft notes that dynamically generated script blocks are logged too, so each layer appears as it runs. Long scripts are split over several 4104 events ('Creating Scriptblock text (1 of N)') that share a ScriptBlock ID: put them back together in order before reading.

distractors.a: Decoding is useful for triage, but stages built at run time are not in the command line.
distractors.b: PSReadLine history records commands typed in interactive consoles, not code passed non-interactively with -EncodedCommand.
distractors.c: Transcription is off unless it is enabled by policy ('Turn on PowerShell Transcription') or started with Start-Transcript; it is not written for every session by default.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know where the deobfuscated code is recorded instead of stopping at the encoded command line.

references.title: Microsoft PowerShell Team: PowerShell the Blue Team
MITRE ATT&CK T1059.001 PowerShell

questions.question: Script block logging is enabled by GPO on a client's Windows 10 host, yet the MSSP finds no 4104 events for the session below. What is the best explanation?
questions.context:
Sysmon Event ID 1, host WS-LEGAL-07
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
CommandLine: powershell.exe -Version 2 -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\Users\Public\s.ps1

Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational: no 4104 events between 09:00 and 11:00
Windows PowerShell log, event 400 at 09:41: ... HostVersion=2.0 ... EngineVersion=2.0 ... HostApplication=powershell.exe -Version 2 -NoProfile ...

options.text: It ran on the PowerShell 2.0 engine, which has no script block logging; event 400 shows the engine version
-ExecutionPolicy Bypass switches off script block logging for the whole session in which it is used on the command line
Script block logging records only commands typed interactively, not scripts started with -File
The 4104 events went to the Sysmon log instead, because Sysmon was installed after the GPO was applied

explanation.correct: Script block logging arrived with PowerShell 5; the 2.0 engine predates it. Where the optional Windows PowerShell 2.0 component and the .NET Framework 3.5 it needs are installed, '-Version 2' runs code without any 4104: a downgrade attack, ATT&CK T1689 Downgrade Attack (T1562.010 before ATT&CK v20). Event 400 in the classic 'Windows PowerShell' log records EngineVersion at engine start, which gives a detection: EngineVersion 2.0, or '-Version 2' in process command lines. Fixes: remove the PowerShell 2.0 component and hunt for the same pattern on other hosts. The missing 4104 is itself a finding to report to the client.

distractors.b: Execution policy only decides which scripts may run; it is not a security boundary and does not control logging.
distractors.c: Script block logging covers commands, script blocks, functions and scripts, whether run interactively or through automation.
distractors.d: Sysmon does not receive PowerShell's events; 4104 is written only to Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat a logging gap as evidence and know how attackers create one.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1689 Downgrade Attack
Microsoft PowerShell Team: PowerShell the Blue Team

questions.subtopic: 4648 explicit credentials on the source host
questions.question: An MSSP analyst sees the 4648 event below on a client workstation. Where should the next query go to learn what adm-sql actually did?
questions.context:
Security log, workstation WS-OPS-12
10:14:07 EventID=4648
  Subject: AccountName=v.stoica LogonID=0x3F2A11
  Account Whose Credentials Were Used: AccountName=adm-sql
  Target Server: TargetServerName=DB-CORE01

options.text: WS-OPS-12's own 4624 events for adm-sql, because 4648 is always followed by a local logon of that account
The domain controllers' 4720 events, because 4648 means adm-sql was created for this connection
DB-CORE01's Security log: 4624 for adm-sql near 10:14 from WS-OPS-12, then follow that session's Logon ID
WS-OPS-12's 4672 events for v.stoica, because 4648 records that v.stoica received adm-sql's privileges locally

explanation.correct: 4648 is written on the computer where a process tried to log on by explicitly supplying an account's credentials (runas, mapping a share with another user, admin tools). It names who supplied them (v.stoica), whose credentials were used (adm-sql) and the target server (DB-CORE01). The resulting session is created on the target, and 4624 is generated on the computer that was accessed. So query DB-CORE01 for 4624 (likely Logon Type 3) for adm-sql at about 10:14 with WS-OPS-12's address, then follow its Logon ID into 4672, share access and process creation on that server, plus authentication events on the domain controllers. Microsoft notes 4648 also occurs routinely (scheduled tasks, runas), so the key question is whether v.stoica should know adm-sql's password at all.

distractors.a: The target server is DB-CORE01, not localhost, so the session for those credentials is created there, not on the workstation.
distractors.b: Account creation is 4720; 4648 uses an account that already exists.
distractors.d: 4648 grants nothing. 4672 is logged where the privileged session is created, which here is the target server.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know on which side of a connection each logon event is written.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: 4648(S) A logon was attempted using explicit credentials
Microsoft Learn: 4624(S) An account was successfully logged on

questions.question: On a software vendor's build agent, a detection rule that looks for Image ending in '\powershell.exe' did not fire for the event below. What does the event show?
questions.context:
Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Create), host BUILD-AG-04
UtcTime: 2026-09-18 02:14:51.233
Image: C:\ProgramData\AgentCache\taskhelper.exe
OriginalFileName: PowerShell.EXE
Company: Microsoft Corporation
CommandLine: taskhelper.exe -nop -w hidden -c <command redacted>
ParentImage: C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
User: CORP\svc-build
Hashes: SHA256=<same hash as powershell.exe on this Windows build>

options.text: A legitimate build helper: the Company field shows the file is signed by Microsoft, so it can be allowed
A renamed PowerShell copy; OriginalFileName comes from the file's version resource, so rules should also match on it
A Sysmon labelling error: OriginalFileName is copied from the parent process, so cmd.exe started PowerShell under the wrong name
File-less execution: the code ran only in memory, and Image is a placeholder path Sysmon writes when no file exists

explanation.correct: OriginalFileName is read from the PE file's version information, which does not change when the file is renamed. Together with a hash equal to the genuine powershell.exe, it identifies a renamed PowerShell copy running from ProgramData under a harmless-looking name: ATT&CK T1036.003 Rename Legitimate Utilities. A rule keyed on the image path misses it; detections should also match OriginalFileName and known hashes. Next: find who created the copy (Sysmon Event ID 11 for that path), what the hidden command did (4104 on this host if script block logging is on), and why svc-build ran it at 02:14.

distractors.a: Company is a text field inside the file, not a signature check. Here the binary is genuine Microsoft code, which is exactly why it is being reused to avoid name-based rules.
distractors.c: OriginalFileName describes the Image file itself; the parent appears separately in ParentImage.
distractors.d: Image is the path of the executable that was started, and a real file exists in ProgramData here.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether your detections still work after a simple rename.

MITRE ATT&CK T1036.003 Rename Legitimate Utilities

questions.question: A bank's detection engineering team is about to enable 'Include command line in process creation events' on all servers and forward 4688 to the SIEM. Which risk must the rollout plan address?

options.text: Enabling the setting disables Sysmon Event ID 1 on the same host, so every Sysmon-based rule will stop firing
Command lines can contain passwords, tokens or client data in clear text, which then sit in the logs and the SIEM
Windows blocks any process whose command line is longer than the audit field can store
Command lines are only recorded for processes started by administrators, so ordinary user activity stays invisible

explanation.correct: Microsoft warns that once the setting is on, anyone who can read the Security events can read the arguments of every process created, and those arguments can include passwords or private data. In a bank that means service-account passwords passed to scripts and tools, connection strings, or customer identifiers in batch jobs, all copied into the SIEM. The plan should therefore restrict access to raw Security logs and SIEM indexes, add a detection for secrets in command lines (each hit means a credential to rotate and a script to fix), and align retention with data-protection rules. Also confirm the advanced audit policy is not overwritten by basic settings (Microsoft points to event 4719 for this).

distractors.a: 4688 and Sysmon are independent sources; enabling one does not affect the other.
distractors.c: Auditing records activity; it never blocks a process.
distractors.d: The command line is logged for every successfully created process, whoever starts it.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you see logging itself as a data-protection risk in a regulated environment.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Command line process auditing

questions.subtopic: logging prerequisites for process and task questions
questions.question: A bank's IR team wants the Windows Security log alone to answer two questions in future cases: 'which command line did the user run?' and 'who created this scheduled task and what does it run?'. Which three settings are required? (Choose 3)

options.text: Audit Process Creation (Detailed Tracking), Success
Audit File System, Success, with a SACL on C:\Windows\System32\Tasks, where Windows stores the task definition files
Administrative Templates\System\Audit Process Creation: 'Include command line in process creation events'
Audit PNP Activity, Success
Audit Other Object Access Events, Success

explanation.correct: Event 4688 exists only if Audit Process Creation is enabled, and its Process Command Line field is filled only when the separate 'Include command line in process creation events' setting is on. Event 4698 (a scheduled task was created), together with 4699-4702 for delete, enable, disable and update, belongs to Audit Other Object Access Events; it records the subject who registered the task and the task's XML, including the command and arguments. Microsoft recommends Success auditing for this subcategory mainly because of these task events. After deployment, check the effective policy with 'auditpol /get /category:*' and make sure basic audit settings do not override the advanced ones.

distractors.b: This would record file access to the task files, not a structured record of the task, its creator and its action; it is not needed when 4698 is enabled.
distractors.d: Audit PNP Activity produces device events such as 6416 (new external device); it says nothing about commands or tasks.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can turn an investigation question into the exact audit settings that answer it.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Audit Other Object Access Events
Microsoft Learn: Command line process auditing
Microsoft Learn: Audit Process Creation

questions.subtopic: evidence that survives a cleared Security log
questions.question: On a client server, the Security log starts with event 1102 at 03:12, logged under account adm-ops, and holds nothing older. Which sources may still contain evidence of what happened on the server before 03:12? (Choose 3)

options.text: Security events already forwarded to the SIEM or a Windows Event Forwarding collector before the clear
The details of the 1102 event, which list the deleted records and their event IDs
The server's Sysmon Operational log, unless it was also cleared (a System-log 104 event would show that)
Authentication events on the domain controllers for adm-ops and for logons to this server
The 4688 event for the clearing command, which Windows writes into the new Security log immediately after 1102

explanation.correct: 1102 records that the Security log was cleared and by whom (the subject's account and Logon ID); nothing else. Every older record in the local Security log is gone, including the 4688 of the clearing command itself, which was written before the clear. Evidence survives elsewhere: copies already forwarded to a SIEM or WEF collector; other logs on the host, such as Sysmon Operational or PowerShell Operational, which are separate files (clearing them leaves event 104 in the System log); and domain controller authentication events for adm-ops and this server. Map it to ATT&CK T1685.005 Clear Windows Event Logs (T1070.001 before ATT&CK v20) and treat adm-ops as compromised until shown otherwise.

distractors.b: 1102 contains only the subject fields (who cleared the log); it holds no list or count of deleted records.
distractors.e: The process that cleared the log was created before the clear, so its 4688 was in the old log and was erased with it.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether a cleared log makes you stop, or makes you look for the copies.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: 1102(S) The audit log was cleared
MITRE ATT&CK T1685.005 Clear Windows Event Logs

questions.subtopic: admin rights in a logon session
questions.question: You need to know whether a remote session on a server ran with administrative rights. Which two pieces of Security log evidence show that? (Choose 2)

options.text: Authentication Package = Kerberos in the session's 4624 event, rather than NTLM
Elevated Token = Yes in the session's 4624 event
Logon Type = 10 in the session's 4624 event
A 4672 event sharing the 4624's Logon ID, listing privileges such as SeDebugPrivilege
Impersonation Level = Impersonation in the session's 4624 event rather than Identification

explanation.correct: Elevated Token = Yes (a 4624 field since Windows 10 / Server 2016) means the session is elevated and has administrator privileges; Microsoft suggests monitoring it to track admin logons. 4672 (special privileges assigned to new logon) is written when sensitive privileges such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege or SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege are given to a new session, and it is linked to the 4624 by Logon ID. Remember that every SYSTEM logon also triggers 4672, so filter machine and service accounts before counting.

distractors.a: Kerberos or NTLM is the authentication protocol; it says nothing about the rights of the session.
distractors.c: Type 10 shows a Remote Desktop logon; standard users in Remote Desktop Users get the same type.

questions.question: Match each Windows Security log event ID to what it tells an analyst.

right.text: A scheduled task was created; the event holds the task's XML, including what it runs

A new service was installed on the system

questions.question: A SaaS company is writing its first Sysmon-based detections. Match each Sysmon event ID to what it records.

A process made a DNS query
A process was created, with command line, hashes and parent process
A DLL (image) was loaded into a process
A registry value was set
A TCP/UDP connection was made, linked to the process that made it

  46 different TargetUserName values, 1 attempt each
  Status=0xC000006D SubStatus=0xC000006A (39 events)

Stale saved credentials on WS-HR-07 retrying against the server; clearing the stored credentials there will stop it
A password spray from WS-HR-07: one try per account across many accounts, then a success for m.ionescu
Seven accounts are locked out (0xC0000064), so the lockout policy has already contained the activity

questions.question: On a bank branch workstation shared by four tellers, you find a Prefetch file showing that an unapproved remote-access tool last ran at 14:32 yesterday. The branch manager wants to know which teller ran it before HR is involved. What is the correct next step?

options.text: Read the user SID stored in the Prefetch file header, which identifies the account that launched it
Name the teller rostered on that workstation at 14:32, since the shift schedule shows who used it
Correlate the run time with logon sessions and process-creation events, as Prefetch stores no user
Check the NTFS owner of the .pf file, because Windows sets it to the account that started the program

In Microsoft Defender XDR, for example: DeviceProcessEvents | where DeviceName == '<host>' and FileName =~ '<tool>.exe' | project Timestamp, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine.

distractors.a: The Prefetch format holds the executable name, run count, run times, volume details and referenced files; there is no user or SID to read.
distractors.b: A roster shows who should have been there, not who launched the program; acting on it before checking logon evidence risks blaming the wrong person in an HR case.
distractors.d: The .pf file is written by the operating system's prefetcher, not by the user's process, so its owner says nothing about who ran the program.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know the limits of each artefact and avoid attributing an action to a person from system-wide evidence.

questions.question: Triaging a client's Windows Server file server, a junior analyst finds C:\Windows\Prefetch empty and drafts the finding 'attacker wiped Prefetch to hide execution'. What should be checked before that finding goes into the client report?

The EnablePrefetcher setting and the USN journal, because application prefetching is often off on servers
Whether running a known tool on the live server now creates a new .pf file in the Prefetch folder
Nothing further, because an empty Prefetch folder is a reliable anti-forensics indicator on any Windows host

explanation.correct: Before calling something anti-forensics, rule out normal configuration. Prefetching is controlled by the EnablePrefetcher value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management\PrefetchParameters (0 disabled, 1 application launch, 2 boot, 3 both), and application prefetching is commonly disabled by default on Windows Server, so an empty folder there can be completely normal. If prefetching is enabled, look for proof of deletion instead of assuming it, such as $UsnJrnl records with a FileDelete reason for *.pf names. Either way, pivot to other execution sources: Amcache, ShimCache, Security 4688 and EDR telemetry.

distractors.a: Finding no carved .pf files is absence of evidence; it fits prefetching never having been enabled just as well as a secure wipe.
distractors.c: Running tools on the live evidence host changes it, and the result only shows today's setting, not what was true during the intrusion; reading the registry value answers this without side effects.
distractors.d: An empty folder is only suspicious where prefetching was enabled; on many servers it is the default state.

explanation.interview_angle: Checking that an artefact should exist before treating its absence as evidence of tampering.

Forensics Wiki: Prefetch

questions.question: An incident response team triages a live host that has not rebooted since an intrusion two days ago. Prefetch shows the attacker's tool ran, yet the AppCompatCache (ShimCache) value in the live SYSTEM hive has no entry for it. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: ShimCache records only programs started through Explorer, so a tool launched from a command shell never appears
ShimCache records only binaries with a valid digital signature, so an unsigned attacker tool is skipped
The attacker must have edited the AppCompatCache value, which should be reported to the client as anti-forensics
New ShimCache entries are kept in memory and written to the registry at shutdown, so they are still only in RAM

explanation.correct: Windows keeps the Application Compatibility Cache in kernel memory and writes it to the AppCompatCache value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache when the system shuts down or restarts. On a host that has not rebooted since the intrusion, the attacker's entries can exist only in RAM. Capture memory and parse it (Volatility 3 has a windows.shimcachemem plugin that reads the cache from ahcache.sys structures). When you read the entries, remember that each timestamp is the file's last-modified time, not an execution time.

distractors.a: That limitation describes UserAssist, which tracks Explorer launches; ShimCache is filled by the application compatibility engine however the program is started.
distractors.b: Signing status does not decide whether a file is cached; signed and unsigned executables both appear.
distractors.c: Tampering is possible, but it is not the first explanation when the cache simply has not been flushed yet; claim anti-forensics only with evidence.

explanation.interview_angle: Knowing when an artefact is written to disk, and that live triage can miss what is still in memory.

references.title: Magnet Forensics: ShimCache vs AmCache
Volatility 3 docs: windows.shimcachemem

questions.question: True or false: on Windows 10 or 11, an InventoryApplicationFile entry in Amcache.hve for C:\Users\Public\svcupd.exe is enough on its own to state in a report that svcupd.exe was executed.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: False. Amcache.hve (C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve) is filled by the compatibility inventory, which also records executables found when directories are scanned or files copied by installers. An entry proves the file was present at that path and gives useful metadata (SHA-1 of roughly the first 31 MB, size, publisher, compile time), not that it ran. Report it as presence, and corroborate execution with Prefetch, Security 4688, EDR process events or other execution artefacts before writing 'executed'. The SHA-1 stays valuable: it survives deletion of the file and can be searched in threat intelligence.

distractors.a: Treating Amcache as an execution log is a common overstatement; on modern Windows it also lists files that were inventoried but never launched.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you separate 'the file existed' from 'the file ran' when writing findings.

references.title: Securelist: AmCache artifact for forensic analysis

questions.question: Match each Windows artefact to what it records.

right.text: Per-user launch count and last-run time, with program names ROT13-encoded
SHA-1 hash, path and publisher details of executables the system inventoried
Folders the user browsed in File Explorer
Run count and up to eight last-run times, plus files touched in the first seconds
File path and the file's own last-modified time, stored in the SYSTEM hive

explanation.correct: Prefetch (C:\Windows\Prefetch) keeps the run count, up to eight last-run times on Windows 8 and later, and the files and folders the program referenced in roughly its first ten seconds. UserAssist (NTUSER.DAT ...\Explorer\UserAssist\{GUID}\Count) is per user and stores ROT13-encoded names with a run count and last-run time. ShimCache (SYSTEM ...\Session Manager\AppCompatCache) lists paths with the file's $STANDARD_INFORMATION last-modified time, which is not an execution time. Amcache.hve stores inventory data including the SHA-1 hash, path and publisher. The unused description, folders browsed in Explorer, belongs to ShellBags.

distractors.l3: The ShimCache timestamp is easily misread as a run time; it is the file's last-modified time, so do not pair ShimCache with 'last-run times'.
distractors.l4: Amcache is not a launch counter; its strength is the SHA-1 hash and file metadata.

Securelist: AmCache artifact for forensic analysis

questions.question: Prefetch shows a memory-dumping utility ran on a workstation at 10:14, while only one user, k.stan, was logged on. k.stan's UserAssist key has no entry for the utility, and a colleague says this clears k.stan. How should you assess that claim?

options.text: It does not clear k.stan: UserAssist tracks Explorer launches, and a tool run from a shell has no entry
It clears k.stan: UserAssist logs every process an account starts, so another account must have run it
It clears k.stan: UserAssist is machine-wide, so a missing entry means nobody ran the tool interactively
It proves k.stan deleted the UserAssist entry, because Windows writes one for every single program launch

explanation.correct: UserAssist (NTUSER.DAT\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\UserAssist\{GUID}\Count) records programs a user launches through the Explorer shell: Start menu, desktop shortcuts, double-click in File Explorer. Programs started from cmd.exe, PowerShell, a script or a remote session do not appear. Its absence therefore neither clears nor implicates k.stan. Attribute the run with the logon session (4624 and its Logon ID), process creation 4688 or EDR telemetry, which record the account and the parent process, for example cmd.exe or powershell.exe.

distractors.b: UserAssist is not a full process log; command-line launches never reach it.
distractors.c: UserAssist lives in each user's NTUSER.DAT, so it is per user, not machine-wide.
distractors.d: Windows does not write UserAssist entries for shell-launched tools, so a missing entry is expected and is not evidence of deletion.

explanation.interview_angle: Testing whether you treat the absence of an artefact as proof without knowing what populates it.

Securelist: UserAssist artifact forensic value

questions.question: In an internal fraud case at a bank, a trader denies ever opening the restricted share folder \\fs01\Treasury\Limits, which was deleted last month. The trader's UsrClass.dat holds a ShellBags entry for that folder. What does this finding support?

options.text: That the trader opened every file that was stored in the folder at the time
Nothing about the trader, because ShellBags are system-wide and shared by all accounts
That the trader's account browsed to the folder, but not which of its files were opened or copied
Nothing, because the entry of a deleted folder is purged, so this one must come from another user

explanation.correct: ShellBags (BagMRU and Bags keys, mainly in UsrClass.dat and also in NTUSER.DAT) store per-user view settings for folders opened in File Explorer, including network shares, removable drives and archives, and they remain after the folder is deleted. An entry in the trader's hive therefore supports that this account navigated to \\fs01\Treasury\Limits. It does not show which files were opened or copied: for that, look at LNK files and Jump Lists in the trader's profile, OpenSavePidlMRU, and the file server's object-access auditing (4663) if it was enabled. Interpret ShellBag timestamps with care, because key last-write times and the folder times embedded in the entry mean different things.

distractors.a: ShellBags record folders, not files; viewing a folder does not mean its files were opened.
distractors.b: ShellBags sit in each user's own hives, which is exactly why they help attribution.
distractors.d: ShellBags persist after a folder is deleted; that persistence is what makes them useful for folders that no longer exist.

explanation.interview_angle: Separating 'viewed a folder' from 'accessed or took files', which matters when evidence may reach HR or a court.

references.title: Binalyze KB: ShellBags
Velociraptor: Windows.Forensics.Shellbags

questions.question: In a bank's investigation of suspected data theft on a USB stick, match each artefact to the question it answers.

right.text: Which drive letter or volume GUID the device was given
Which files were copied onto the device
Which vendor, product and instance ID (serial, if reported) the device has
When the device was first installed on this computer
Which user account had the device's volume mounted

explanation.correct: USBSTOR (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USBSTOR) identifies the storage device by vendor, product, revision and instance ID. MountedDevices maps drive letters (\DosDevices\E:) and volume GUIDs to that device. MountPoints2, in each user's NTUSER.DAT, lists the volume GUIDs that account had mounted, which is how you tie the device to a user. setupapi.dev.log records the driver installation the first time the device was connected; its times are local time, unlike the UTC times in the registry. None of these records which files were copied: that needs endpoint DLP or EDR telemetry, or analysis of the device itself.

distractors.l2: MountedDevices is system-wide; it shows the drive letter but not which user used the device, which is MountPoints2's role.
distractors.l1: USBSTOR identifies the device; it does not list files written to it, so no registry key answers 'which files were copied'.

explanation.interview_angle: Building a USB timeline from several artefacts, each answering one question.

MITRE ATT&CK T1052.001 Exfiltration over USB

questions.question: A user says a colleague deleted her report from a shared PC. In C:\$Recycle.Bin\S-1-5-21-1844237615-456123789-3012345678-1107\ you find $I8K2QWE.docx and $R8K2QWE.docx. What do these files tell you?

options.text: $I8K2QWE.docx is the recoverable document itself, while $R8K2QWE.docx records its original path and deletion time
$R holds the content, $I the original path, size and deletion time; the SID folder shows which account deleted it
The report was permanently deleted from the volume, so its content can now only be recovered by carving unallocated space
Nothing about who deleted it, because all accounts on the PC write their deleted files into one shared Recycle Bin folder

explanation.correct: Since Windows Vista, each deleted item goes to C:\$Recycle.Bin\<SID>\ as a pair with the same random suffix: the $R file is the content (renamed, otherwise intact) and the $I file is the metadata: original full path, file size and deletion time. The folder is named after the SID of the account that deleted the file; resolve it (for example through the ProfileList key in the SOFTWARE hive or the domain) to an account name. That shows which account deleted the file, not which person was at the keyboard, so pair it with logon evidence. Files removed with Shift+Delete or from a command line skip the Recycle Bin entirely.

distractors.a: The roles are reversed: $R is the content and $I is the metadata.
distractors.c: The $R file still holds the full content, so the report is recoverable straight from the Recycle Bin folder.
distractors.d: Each account gets its own subfolder named after its SID, which is what allows attribution.

references.title: Velociraptor: Windows.Forensics.RecycleBin

questions.subtopic: Volume shadow copies: earlier registry state
questions.question: In a bank insider case, the employee ran a registry-cleaning utility the day before the laptop was seized, and USBSTOR in the imaged SYSTEM hive now lists no storage devices. Which source can give you the pre-cleaning registry hives themselves?

options.text: Volume shadow copies in the image that predate the cleaning, exposed read-only and parsed
The $UsnJrnl, which keeps a copy of the registry keys and values the cleaner removed from the hive
The cleaning utility's own undo feature, run on the seized laptop to restore the removed entries
The pagefile, which holds a complete copy of every registry hive each time Windows writes the hive

explanation.correct: Volume Shadow Copy snapshots (restore points, backups, update checkpoints) are block-level copy-on-write images of the volume, so a snapshot older than the cleaning contains the SYSTEM and NTUSER.DAT hives as they were then. List the snapshots in the image, expose them read-only on a forensic workstation (for example with libvshadow's vshadowmount) and parse USBSTOR, MountedDevices and MountPoints2 from each. Snapshots exist only if System Protection or backups created them, and attackers often delete them (vssadmin delete shadows, ATT&CK T1490), so also check sources the cleaner may have missed, such as setupapi.dev.log.

distractors.b: The USN journal records that files changed and why, not registry content; Microsoft notes it cannot be used to reverse a change.
distractors.c: Running tools on the original evidence alters it and undermines the integrity of the case; work only on the verified image.
distractors.d: pagefile.sys holds paged-out memory fragments; pieces of the registry may turn up there, but not a complete hive from a known point in time.

explanation.interview_angle: Knowing where historical state survives anti-forensics, and preserving integrity while you recover it.

Microsoft Learn: Volume Shadow Copy Service
MITRE ATT&CK T1070 Indicator Removal

questions.subtopic: Cloud upload: identifying the uploaded file
questions.question: Proxy logs at a bank show a 48 MB HTTPS upload from a dealer's workstation to a personal cloud-storage site at 18:22, and the browser history confirms a visit to the site's upload page. Which host artefact is most likely to name the file the dealer selected for upload?

options.text: The downloads table in the browser's History database, which logs files transferred in both directions
OpenSavePidlMRU in the dealer's NTUSER.DAT, which records files picked in the Open/Save dialog
The Prefetch file for the browser executable, whose referenced-files list includes uploaded files
The UserAssist entry for the browser, whose focus time and count show which file was handled

explanation.correct: When a website asks for a file, the browser shows the Windows common Open dialog, and the shell records the selection under NTUSER.DAT\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\ComDlg32\OpenSavePidlMRU (a subkey per extension plus '*' for all), while LastVisitedPidlMRU ties the browser executable to the folder it used. Line the MRU entry and the key's last-write time up with the 18:22 proxy record. Limits: a drag-and-drop upload bypasses the dialog, the MRU proves selection rather than a completed transfer, and without TLS inspection the proxy sees only the destination and byte counts, so confirm with cloud-provider or CASB logs where available.

distractors.a: The browser's downloads table records downloads only; uploads are not logged there.
distractors.c: Prefetch lists files referenced in roughly the first ten seconds after the browser starts, not files chosen later in a session.
distractors.d: UserAssist counts program launches and focus time; it holds no names of files a program handled.

explanation.interview_angle: Reconstructing a cloud upload from host artefacts, and stating what each one cannot prove.

MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
Microsoft Learn: Common Item Dialog

questions.subtopic: LNK files: which timestamp means what
questions.question: You parse budget_2027.xlsx.lnk from a client user's Recent folder. The LNK file's own NTFS times are created 2026-09-01 09:10 and modified 2026-09-29 16:45. The target times embedded in the LNK are created 2025-11-03 08:00 and modified 2026-09-28 18:02. Which statement is best supported?

options.text: The user first opened the spreadsheet on 2025-11-03, the creation time recorded for the target
The user edited the spreadsheet on 2026-09-28 at 18:02, because the LNK records the user's own edits
The spreadsheet was deleted on 2026-09-29 at 16:45, which is when the LNK file was last modified
The user first opened the file through the shell around 2026-09-01 and last around 2026-09-29 16:45

explanation.correct: A Recent-folder LNK is created the first time the user opens a file of that name through the shell and updated on later opens, so its own creation and modification times approximate the first and last open. The target times in the LNK header (CreationTime, AccessTime and WriteTime in the MS-SHLLINK format) are a snapshot of the target file's own timestamps when the link was last updated: they describe the file, not the user. The LNK also stores the target's path, size, volume serial number and drive type, and it survives deletion of the target.

distractors.a: The embedded creation time belongs to the file itself, wherever it was created; it is not the user's first open.
distractors.b: The embedded modified time is the file's last write before the latest open; it does not say who wrote it.
distractors.c: An update to the LNK reflects another open of the file; deleting the target does not touch the LNK.

explanation.interview_angle: Reading artefact timestamps for what they actually measure instead of the first plausible meaning.

references.title: Microsoft MS-SHLLINK: ShellLinkHeader
Forensics Wiki: LNK

questions.question: An attacker's 350-byte batch script was deleted from an NTFS volume, and carving unallocated clusters did not find it. Where else might its full content survive?

options.text: In the $UsnJrnl, which stores the data written to each file alongside its change record
In the $Recycle.Bin $R file, since every deletion on NTFS passes through the Recycle Bin
In its old $MFT record, because small files are stored resident inside the record itself
In the Prefetch folder, which keeps a cached copy of every script the system has run

explanation.correct: Each NTFS file has a record (usually 1,024 bytes) in the $MFT. When the content is small enough, typically up to several hundred bytes, it is stored resident in the record's $DATA attribute instead of in separate clusters, so carving unallocated clusters will never find it. Deleting the file only marks the record as free; until NTFS reuses that record, its name ($FILE_NAME), timestamps and resident content can be recovered by parsing the $MFT, including the unallocated entries.

distractors.a: The change journal records the file name, reason flags and time of each change, not the data; Microsoft notes it cannot be used to reverse a change.
distractors.b: Command-line deletion, Shift+Delete and script-driven deletion bypass the Recycle Bin.
distractors.d: Prefetch files hold execution metadata and referenced paths, not copies of scripts; at most the script's path may appear among the files referenced by CMD.EXE's Prefetch entry.

explanation.interview_angle: Understanding NTFS internals well enough to know where deleted content can still sit.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Master File Table
Microsoft Learn: Change Journal Records

questions.question: A macro-enabled workbook sent to a bank's payments team contains a lure sheet listing real customer IBANs. An analyst wants to upload it to a free public online sandbox to speed up triage. What should happen instead?

options.text: Search the hash first, then use an internal or private sandbox, because public uploads can be shared
Upload it anyway, because public sandboxes delete each sample as soon as the analysis report is produced
Open it on the analyst's own workstation with macros disabled to read the code quickly without risk
Forward it to all staff as an example so that everyone can recognise the lure if it arrives again

explanation.correct: Public analysis services may make submitted files and reports available to other users and partners: VirusTotal, for example, states that the contents of submitted files may be shared with premium customers. Uploading this workbook would disclose customer data, which is a potential personal-data breach in itself, and can tell the attacker, who may watch for their sample, that the lure was caught. Look the hash up first (a lookup sends no content), then analyse in an internal or contracted private sandbox, and record the handling in the case notes.

distractors.b: Public services keep and share samples; deletion after analysis is not the default and usually needs a separate request.
distractors.c: Opening live malware on a production workstation risks infection even with macros disabled, and it is not an isolated analysis environment.
distractors.d: Forwarding the live sample spreads both the malware and the customer data; awareness messages use sanitised screenshots.

explanation.interview_angle: Balancing triage speed against data protection and operational security in a regulated bank.

references.title: VirusTotal docs: How it works
NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1: Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling

questions.question: Your automated triage pipeline marked a loader 'clean'. Its sandbox report shows it slept for about ten minutes, queried the disk size and the network adapter's MAC address, then exited with no network traffic. What should the pipeline engineer change?

options.text: Nothing, because a sample that makes no network connection in the sandbox cannot be a working loader
Block every file that calls a sleep function, since long sleeps are a reliable indicator of malware
Raise the sandbox's CPU count, because processor count is the only environment check loaders perform
Treat it as possible sandbox evasion: rerun with a realistic VM, longer runtime and user activity

explanation.correct: Long sleeps and checks of disk size, MAC address vendor prefixes, CPU count or user activity are classic virtualisation and sandbox evasion (ATT&CK T1497, with sub-techniques for system checks, user activity checks and time-based evasion). 'No behaviour' is inconclusive, not clean. Re-run with a hardened profile (realistic disk size, non-virtual MAC prefix, longer runtime or sleep acceleration, simulated mouse and document activity), add static and memory analysis, and make the pipeline label such results 'evasive or inconclusive' instead of 'clean'.

distractors.a: Evasive malware deliberately stays quiet when it suspects analysis; no traffic is exactly what it wants the sandbox to report.
distractors.b: Legitimate software sleeps all the time; blocking on that alone would cause mass false positives.
distractors.c: Processor count is one of many checks; this report shows disk-size and MAC checks that a CPU change would not address.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you understand sandbox limits and design triage that does not equate silence with safety.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1497 Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion
MITRE ATT&CK T1497.001 System Checks

questions.question: Which THREE kinds of evidence can a memory capture of a running laptop provide that a disk image taken after shutdown usually cannot? (Choose three.)

options.text: Network connections open at capture time, with the owning process
Prefetch files recording the programs that ran on the laptop last week
Code injected into a running process that has no file on disk
MFT records of files deleted yesterday
Keys of an encrypted volume that is currently unlocked

explanation.correct: RAM holds the live state of the system: open network connections with their owning process (a netscan-style plugin lists them), code injected into processes or loaded only in memory (fileless malware), decrypted data, and the keys of encrypted volumes that are mounted and unlocked. All of this is lost at shutdown, apart from fragments that may land in pagefile.sys or hiberfil.sys. Prefetch files and $MFT records live on disk and survive a normal shutdown, so the disk image already contains them. This is why memory is captured first on a running system.

distractors.b: Prefetch files live in C:\Windows\Prefetch on disk and are collected in the disk image.
distractors.d: Deleted-file records stay in the $MFT on disk until reused, so the disk image captures them.

explanation.interview_angle: Explaining why memory is captured before a system is powered off.

references.title: NIST SP 800-86: Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
Volatility 3 docs: Windows plugins

questions.question: A bank is investigating whether a departing relationship manager copied a client portfolio file to a USB stick, which security has now seized. Which TWO sources can show the file being written to the stick, rather than only that the stick was connected or browsed? (Choose two.)

options.text: The USBSTOR key showing the stick's last connection time during the employee's final working day
Endpoint DLP or EDR telemetry recording a file copy or write to removable media
A LNK file in the user's Recent folder pointing to E:\Clients\portfolio.xlsx
The seized stick's own file-system entry for portfolio.xlsx, created during that session
A ShellBags entry showing that the user browsed E:\Clients in File Explorer

explanation.correct: Host registry and shell artefacts show connection (USBSTOR, MountedDevices, MountPoints2), browsing (ShellBags) or opening (LNK files, Jump Lists), but none of them records a write. Two sources can. First, endpoint telemetry that logs file activity to removable media: Microsoft Purview Endpoint DLP, for example, can audit 'Copy to USB removable device' for protected files. Second, the stick itself: imaged with a write blocker, its file system shows portfolio.xlsx with a creation time that, after a normal Windows copy, reflects when it was written there, while the modified time is carried over from the source. Compare the file's hash with the original on the bank's share. If the 'Audit Removable Storage' policy was enabled, Security log object-access events (4663) on the removable volume can add a third, host-side record of the write.

distractors.a: USBSTOR proves the device was connected, not what was written to it.
distractors.c: A Recent LNK shows the file was opened from E:, so it existed on the stick, but not that this workstation wrote it there.
distractors.e: ShellBags show that a folder was viewed; they say nothing about files written into it.

explanation.interview_angle: Distinguishing connection, browsing and opening from actual data transfer when the stakes are an insider case.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1052.001 Exfiltration over USB
Microsoft Learn: Learn about Endpoint DLP
Elcomsoft: USB device forensics on Windows 10 and 11

questions.question: At a client, an attacker emptied a staging folder of compressed archives, C:\PerfLogs\stage\, with Shift+Delete yesterday. Which TWO artefacts on the C: volume may still reveal the deleted archive names? (Choose two.)

options.text: $I files in C:\$Recycle.Bin\<SID>\ for the attacker's account
$UsnJrnl:$J records with a FileDelete reason for those names
Security log 4624 events for the account that was logged on at the time
$MFT records marked not in use that still hold a $FILE_NAME attribute
UserAssist entries in the attacker account's NTUSER.DAT

explanation.correct: Shift+Delete bypasses the Recycle Bin, so there are no $I and $R pairs. NTFS still remembers. The USN change journal ($Extend\$UsnJrnl:$J) logs each file's name, parent folder reference, time and reason flags such as FileCreate, RenameNewName and FileDelete, as long as the journal has not wrapped; it is size-limited, so collect it quickly. The $MFT record of each deleted file is only marked free, and until it is reused it keeps the $FILE_NAME attribute (name, parent, timestamps). Parse both from a forensic image, for example with MFTECmd, and build a timeline of the staging activity.

distractors.a: Shift+Delete removes files without moving them to the Recycle Bin, so no $I metadata files are created.
distractors.c: Event 4624 records logons, not file names; object-access auditing (4663) would be needed, and only if it was configured for that folder.
distractors.e: UserAssist records programs launched through Explorer, not files that were deleted.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Change Journal Records
Microsoft Learn: Master File Table
MITRE ATT&CK T1070.004 File Deletion

questions.question: Order these evidence sources from most volatile to least volatile, following the order of volatility in RFC 3227.

options.text: Data on the local disk
CPU registers and cache
Remote logging and monitoring data
Routing table, ARP cache, process table and memory
Archival media such as backup tapes
Temporary file systems

explanation.correct: RFC 3227 tells collectors to start with the evidence that disappears first: registers and cache, then the routing table, ARP cache, process table, kernel statistics and memory, then temporary file systems, then disk, then remote logging and monitoring data, then physical configuration and network topology, and finally archival media. In practice an analyst cannot read CPU registers directly, so the first real step on a running system is a memory capture, before anything that changes or powers off the host. Remote logs rank below the local disk because they sit on separate systems with their own retention.
explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can justify collection order instead of reciting it.

references.title: RFC 3227: Guidelines for Evidence Collection and Archiving

questions.question: An MSSP responder arrives at a client's running workstation suspected of compromise, and the client has approved a full forensic collection. Put the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Compute the image hash and verify it against the acquisition hash
Capture physical memory to external forensic media
Record the system time, screen state and who is present in the chain-of-custody notes
Analyse a working copy of the image, never the original
Acquire a forensic image of the disk

explanation.correct: Document first, without touching the system: note the system time against a reference clock, what is on screen and who is present, and open the chain-of-custody record. Then capture RAM, the most volatile evidence, to external media with a trusted tool (writing to the suspect disk would overwrite evidence). Next acquire the disk image, live or after shutdown with a write blocker depending on encryption and the agreed plan. Hash the image, verify it matches the acquisition hash and record it in the custody log, and only then analyse a working copy so the original stays untouched.
explanation.interview_angle: Showing you protect evidence integrity and volatility under time pressure at a client site.

references.title: NIST SP 800-86: Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
RFC 3227: Guidelines for Evidence Collection and Archiving

questions.question: You are designing the triage workflow for suspicious files collected by an EDR product. Put the steps in a sound order.

options.text: Detonate the sample in an isolated sandbox restored from a clean snapshot
Look up the file hash in internal and threat-intelligence sources without uploading the file
Turn the confirmed indicators into detections and hunt for them across the estate
Run static triage: true file type, strings, imports, signature and packer checks
Review the sandbox report: process tree, network activity, files and registry keys changed

explanation.correct: Start with what is cheapest and discloses nothing: a hash lookup can settle a known sample in seconds without sharing the file. Static triage comes next (true file type, strings, imports, digital signature, packing) and tells you what to expect and how to configure detonation. Then run the sample in an isolated sandbox reverted to a clean snapshot, and review its behaviour: process tree, network connections, dropped files, registry and persistence changes. Only then convert the confirmed indicators (hashes, domains, mutexes, behaviours) into detections and hunt across all endpoints for other infections.

questions.question: Match each Volatility-style memory analysis plugin to its purpose.

right.text: Show the arguments each process was started with
Recover processes that already exited by scanning for process structures
Flag executable, writable process memory with no file behind it
Recover local account password hashes from registry hives in memory
List network endpoints and connections with the owning process
List the modules each process loaded, from its own loader list

explanation.correct: In Volatility 3 these are windows.malfind (also exposed under windows.malware.malfind in recent releases), windows.netscan, windows.cmdline, windows.dlllist and windows.hashdump. malfind looks for memory regions that are private (not backed by a file) with execute and write permissions, a common sign of injected code. netscan scans for TCP and UDP endpoint objects and reports their owning process. cmdline reads each process's command line from its PEB. dlllist walks the loader's module list in the PEB, so a DLL unlinked by malware can be missing there (compare with ldrmodules). hashdump reads the SAM and SYSTEM hives cached in memory. The unused description, finding exited processes, belongs to psscan.

distractors.l4: dlllist trusts the process's own loader list, so it is not the plugin that finds hidden or injected code; that is malfind or ldrmodules.

explanation.interview_angle: Knowing which question each memory plugin answers, so you can plan an analysis instead of running everything.

Volatility 3 docs: windows.malfind

questions.question: Match each NTUSER.DAT key to the user activity it records.

right.text: Search terms typed into File Explorer's search box
Commands typed into the Win+R Run dialog
Programs launched from the Start menu, with run counts
Paths typed into File Explorer's address bar
Files and folders recently opened through the shell, also listed per extension
The program that used an Open/Save dialog and the folder it last used there

explanation.correct: All five live under NTUSER.DAT\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\, which makes them per-user evidence. It ran three times from Users\Public\Tools and read a config in m.ionescu's profile; upload is unproven
It was started from a USB stick, because the record lists a volume with its own serial number
The three times are file-modification times of RCLONE.EXE, so the record does not establish execution

That makes exfiltration to cloud storage (ATT&CK T1567.002) a strong hypothesis, but Prefetch records no network activity, destination or data volume. Prove the transfer with proxy or firewall logs (bytes out to the cloud provider at those times), the remote definitions in rclone.conf and any cloud-side logs; attribute the account with logon, 4688 or EDR records, because Prefetch itself holds no user.

distractors.c: The same volume GUID and serial also hold \WINDOWS\SYSTEM32, so this is the system volume, not removable media.
distractors.d: These are run times recorded by the prefetcher; the file-modification-time trap belongs to ShimCache.

questions.question: An MSSP analyst reviewing a client server pulls this $MFT entry for a DLL flagged by threat hunting. What is the most defensible reading?

options.text: The DLL has existed since 2019, and Windows refreshes the $FILE_NAME times every time the file is read
The entry is corrupt, because $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME times must always be identical
The Record changed time of 23:14:09 is when a user last opened the DLL, so someone loaded it at that time
It arrived at about 23:13:47 on 2 October 2026 and its $SI times were set back later; 2019 is unreliable

explanation.correct: $STANDARD_INFORMATION timestamps can be set from user mode (for example with the SetFileTime API), which is how timestomping tools work; $FILE_NAME timestamps are maintained by the NTFS driver and are much harder to change. Here $FILE_NAME says the file was created at 23:13:47 on 2 October 2026, $SI claims 2019 with zeroed sub-second values, and the $SI record-changed time, 22 seconds after creation, shows when the metadata was rewritten. That pattern fits timestomping (ATT&CK T1070.006). Corroborate before concluding: look for a BasicInfoChange record in $UsnJrnl at 23:14:09 and for the process that wrote the file, since extraction from an archive can also leave old $SI times.

distractors.a: NTFS does not update $FILE_NAME times when a file is read; they are set at creation and by certain operations such as rename or move.
distractors.b: $SI and $FN often differ after normal file operations; a mismatch is a lead, not corruption.
distractors.c: The record-changed time marks a change to the MFT entry's metadata, not an open or a load.

explanation.interview_angle: Spotting timestomping from $SI versus $FN, and knowing how to corroborate it before reporting.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1070.006 Timestomp
Microsoft Learn: File Times
Forensics Wiki: Timestomp

options.text: The spreadsheet was renamed to a .jpg, an archive was created and filled, and both were deleted outright at 17:09
The spreadsheet's contents were copied into photos.7z, so the archive certainly contains the client data
Both files were sent to the Recycle Bin at 17:09 and can still be restored from the user's C:\$Recycle.Bin folder
Two separate new files, Q3_HNW_clients.xlsx and holiday_2019.jpg, were both created at 17:02:11

A Recycle Bin deletion would instead appear as a rename into $Recycle.Bin, so this was a permanent delete (T1070.004). The journal records names and reasons, not content or destination: check 7-Zip execution (Prefetch, Amcache), what happened between 17:03 and 17:09 (browser, proxy and USB artefacts), and try to recover the archive from unallocated space or shadow copies.

distractors.c: A Recycle Bin deletion shows up as a rename into $Recycle.Bin with $I/$R names, not as FileDelete.
distractors.d: Old and new names on the same entry in the same second are the two halves of one rename, not two new files.

Enum\USBSTOR\Disk&Ven_Generic&Prod_Flash_Disk&Rev_8.07\7&1f3c9a2&0

MountedDevices
    \DosDevices\E:  ->  _??_USBSTOR#Disk&Ven_Generic&Prod_Flash_Disk&Rev_8.07#7&1f3c9a2&0#{53f56307-b6bf-11d0-94f2-00a0c91efb8b}
    \??\Volume{c4a1e6f0-3b2d-11f0-9a1c-806e6f6e6963}  ->  (same data as \DosDevices\E:)

NTUSER.DAT (d.marin)

options.text: Read the stick's hardware serial number and compare it with 7&1f3c9a2, which is the device's serial
Plug the stick into a forensic workstation; if that machine also reports 7&1f3c9a2&0, it is the same stick
Not by serial: the '&' as second character means Windows generated this ID, so match the volume serial
No link can be made, because the '&0' suffix shows the stick was never connected after its first install

explanation.correct: A device that reports a unique serial shows it as the USBSTOR instance ID. When the second character is '&', as in 7&1f3c9a2&0, the stick did not report a unique serial and the Plug and Play manager built an ID that is unique only on this system (it can even change with the USB port used), so it cannot be compared with the physical stick or another computer. Link them through the volume instead: image the stick with a write blocker and read its volume serial number, then find that serial in LNK files, Jump Lists or Partition/Diagnostic mount events on the laptop, and combine it with MountedDevices (E:) and MountPoints2 in d.marin's NTUSER.DAT, which show this account had the volume mounted. Reformatting the stick changes the volume serial, so record it before anything else touches the device.

distractors.a: There is no hardware serial to compare: the '&' marks an ID that Windows generated.
distractors.b: A generated ID depends on the host and port, so another machine will produce a different value even for the same stick, and connecting it there also writes new artefacts.
distractors.d: The trailing '&0' is part of the instance ID format, not a connection counter.

explanation.interview_angle: Knowing when a USB 'serial number' is not evidence of a specific physical device.

questions.question: In a memory image, these two processes appear in psscan output but not in pslist. Which reading is most defensible?
questions.context:
windows.pslist (excerpt)
PID   PPID  ImageFileName  CreateTime (UTC)     ExitTime
4     0     System         2026-10-20 07:58:12  N/A
612   488   services.exe   2026-10-20 07:58:19  N/A
3120  2984  explorer.exe   2026-10-20 08:04:51  N/A

windows.psscan (rows with no match in pslist)
PID   PPID  ImageFileName  CreateTime (UTC)     ExitTime
5584  3120  cmd.exe        2026-10-20 09:12:03  2026-10-20 09:12:09
6012  3120  svchost.exe    2026-10-20 09:40:17  N/A

options.text: Both are hidden by a rootkit, since any psscan row that is missing from pslist means the process was unlinked
5584 simply exited; 6012 has no exit time, is off the active list and has the wrong parent: examine it
Both are normal leftovers of exited processes, so psscan rows absent from pslist need no further work
6012 is a legitimate service host, because svchost.exe is a standard Windows process image name

explanation.correct: pslist walks the kernel's list of active processes (the ActiveProcessLinks in each EPROCESS), while psscan scans memory for process structures, so it also finds processes that have exited and processes unlinked from the list to hide them (direct kernel object manipulation, a rootkit technique, ATT&CK T1014). PID 5584 has an exit time: a short-lived cmd.exe, which is expected to appear only in psscan (its activity is still worth checking). PID 6012 has no exit time, is missing from the active list, and is an svchost.exe whose parent is explorer.exe instead of services.exe (PID 612). Examine it further (malfind, dlllist, handles, netscan) and dump it, and remember psscan can also surface stale structures, so corroborate before declaring a rootkit.

distractors.a: Exited processes are the most common reason for psscan-only rows, and 5584 has an exit time.
distractors.c: 6012 has no exit time and an anomalous parent; dismissing every psscan-only row would miss hidden processes.
distractors.d: Malware often reuses system process names; a genuine svchost.exe is started by services.exe, not by explorer.exe.

explanation.interview_angle: Knowing how two plugins enumerate processes differently and what each difference implies.
